title: Trust Region Policy Distillation
claim: Direct supervision from a distant target is unstable; interpolating toward it creates a nearby intermediate target that keeps updates within a safe region.
layout: Single panel, circle region with outside target, dashed vs solid arrows, formula at right
description: A single geometric diagram. A large beige circle labeled "Trust Region" holds the current student policy π_student^(t) near its center. Outside the circle at upper right sits π_teacher. A red dashed arrow labeled "Naive OPD" curves from the teacher into the student, crossing the circle boundary to show a large, unstable jump. A solid blue line runs from the teacher, and a short blue arrow runs from the student, to a blue point inside the circle at the bottom, π̃_teacher^(t). A blue formula at right gives this point as α π_teacher + (1−α) π_student^(t). An orange dashed arrow labeled "TOP-D" runs from π̃_teacher^(t) back up to the student. The eye goes first to the circle and the red arrow.
caption: While standard OPD forces direct teacher supervision and suffers from unstable optimization, TOP-D ensures stable training by dynamically constructing a proximal teacher at every iteration.
abstract: Big goals are hard to achieve all at once; breaking them into small steps is wiser. We present Trust Region Policy Distillation (TOP-D), which transforms the notoriously unstable, high-variance On-Policy Distillation (OPD) into a stable training paradigm by dynamically constructing a proximal teacher. Theoretically, we establish a rigorous framework demonstrating that TOP-D inherently controls gradient variance. By providing a formal global convergence analysis alongside a monotonic improvement bound, we mathematically formalize the reliability and stability of the overall training dynamics. Empirically, TOP-D dramatically enhances training stability, sample efficiency, and final performance on mathematical reasoning tasks. More importantly, TOP-D introduces zero additional computational overhead, positioning itself as a promising alternative to the well-established OPD paradigm.
